title: Syndicate gets concession to dam the Litani for Tyre-Sidon irrigation
why: The Handbook says plans were drawn for a dam eight miles from the sea, but the scheme fell through and the river's power stayed unused.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 404

title: Tramway concession granted for a Sidon-Tripoli line of 115 km
why: Awarded to a local, M. Khadra; the Beirut-Ma'amiltein section was built first and the Sidon-Beirut stretch needed a road first.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), pp. 552-553

title: Wassa Pasha makes Jounieh second capital of Kesrouan
why: He built a serai for public services; Jounieh then grew from 5,000 people to over 10,000 by 1906, all Maronite.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 546

title: First permanent Maronite priest arrives in New York
why: Rev. Betros Korkemaz established the first Maronite mission in New York, under the local Catholic bishops.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 106

title: Beirut-Damascus diligence leaves at 4 a.m., fares 145 and 101 piastres
why: Murray's 1892 handbook calls the French company's road the finest anywhere; a night coach left at 6 p.m. and reached Damascus at 8.30 a.m.
actors: Compagnie de la route de Beyrouth a Damas
cite: Murray, Handbook for Travellers in Syria and Palestine (1892), pp. 304-305

title: Locust swarms hit Syria; Beirut residents ordered to gather them
why: Jessup says in Aleppo the governor demanded every man bring a measure of locusts, 5,500 tons by the official count; Beirut crowds were sent out.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 586

title: Wassa Pasha dies; council president holds the governor's powers
why: The Porte entrusted the Central Administrative Council's president with interim authority, a precedent used again in 1907.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 514; Jessup vol. II p. 585
dup_of: Wasa Pasha dies in office; Naoum Pasha becomes mutasarrif

title: Beirut-Damascus road company dissolves into the railway company
why: The Société du chemin de fer ottoman économique de Beyrouth-Damas-Hauran absorbed it; the Batignolles company got the works.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 551

title: Powers' protocol makes Naoum Pasha apply the 1864 Reglement strictly
why: It asked for free Central Council elections, the 1864 court system restored and magistrates protected from arbitrary removal.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 528 and note 1

title: Naoum Pasha arrives to take over as governor of Mount Lebanon
why: Jessup records his arrival on 4 September, some weeks after the 15 August protocol that set the terms of his rule.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 585
dup_of: Wasa Pasha dies in office; Naoum Pasha becomes mutasarrif

title: Ground broken in Beirut for the Beirut-Damascus railway
why: Jessup and Jouplain agree on the date; twelve sheep were sacrificed at the ceremony; Batignolles ran the works, done in under two years.
cite: Jessup vol. II p. 585; Jouplain p. 551

title: Chicago exposition becomes 'first general bugle call' for Syrian emigration
why: Hitti dates the move to mass emigration to the early 1890s; Zahle was a source from the early 1880s.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 48

title: HMS Victoria sinks off Tripoli after collision with HMS Camperdown
why: The British Mediterranean fleet had spent five days off Beirut; Jessup counts 375 dead, including Admiral Tryon.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 598 (375 dead); Wikipedia, HMS Victoria (1887), gives 358

title: Fire destroys the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus
why: Jessup says the event deeply stirred Moslems and might have led to another massacre; the Sultan ordered it rebuilt.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 600

title: Mary Pierson Eddy gets first Ottoman medical permit issued to a woman
why: Jessup says it was on the same terms as men; she then ran clinics at Ma'amiltein and travelled by camp across Mount Lebanon.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), pp. 597-598

title: Beirut-Damascus railway inaugurated with ceremony
why: Jouplain dates the opening to 1 March 1894; Wikipedia and the existing timeline say 1895, and Baedeker and the Admiralty Handbook say 1896.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 552
dup_of: Beirut-Damascus railway (147 km) built and opened

title: Damascus-Mzerib line inaugurated
why: The branch ran towards the Hauran and was planned to extend to Mecca for pilgrim traffic.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 552

title: Holy Synod sends Raphael Hawaweeny to lead Syrian Orthodox in America
why: At the Syrians' request, the Russian synod sent the Syrian priest, later bishop (d. 1915), with headquarters at Brooklyn.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 107

title: E. G. Freyer arrives to run the American Press in Beirut
why: He took up the posts of press manager and mission treasurer; he married in Cairo on 3 December that year.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 611

title: Hauran Druze revolt of 1895-96 ends in settlement
why: Druzes of the Hauran had been largely independent; after the 1896 settlement they kept only exemption from military service.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 243

title: Saint Joseph University medical diplomas begin to qualify holders in France
why: The Handbook dates this to about 1896; the school was set up in 1883 with French government help and degree powers date from 1881.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 200

title: Founders meet in Beirut to plan the Asfuriyeh hospital for the insane
why: Theophilus Waldmeier's plan led to the Lebanon Hospital for Mental Diseases at Asfuriyeh; Jessup was committee secretary.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 521; also p. 623 which gives 18 April

title: Scarlet fever reaches Beirut, blamed on returning emigrants
why: Jessup says it first appeared in May 1896 and also hit Zahle, thought to have come in the baggage of emigrants back from America.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 623

title: Hauran Druzes rise and destroy two Ottoman battalions
why: They tore up railway track and telegraph; 2,500 troops were brought from Macedonia. Jessup blames the troops' treatment of Druze women.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), pp. 623-624

title: US consul Thomas Gibson dies of smallpox in Beirut
why: He died in the Knights of St John hospital; he had sent the warship Marblehead to Alexandretta in April to free a missionary.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 623

title: About 1,000 Syrian immigrants reach Argentina in one year
why: Argentine official figures: about 1,000 for all of 1880-90, under 100 a year from 1890 to 1897, then 1,000 in 1897.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 187

title: American Press catalogue lists 601 titles; 590 million pages printed to date
why: Statistics for 1897 also show the Syrian Protestant College at 309 students and 164 collegiate graduates by 1896-97.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 641

title: Naoum Pasha's term as governor renewed
why: Jouplain notes the Porte renewed his five-year term in 1897; no governor served beyond ten years in practice.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 514

title: First Brummana conference of Christian workers opens
why: About 196 people from missions across the empire met 9 to 14 August at the Friends' Mission in Brummana on Mount Lebanon.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 651

title: 3,708 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1899
why: First year the US counted Syrians apart from 'Turkey in Asia'; Mount Lebanon was the chief source.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Dog River flood sweeps away road and railway bridges
why: Jessup says the winter rains burst the Lebanon gorges and destroyed the stone wagon bridge and iron railway bridge at the river mouth.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 682

title: 56,909 Syrians admitted to the US in twelve years
why: Of these 38,635 (67.9%) were male and 18,274 (32.1%) female, per the Immigration Commission figures Hitti cites.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 58

title: US admits 89,971 Syrian immigrants in 21 years
why: Hitti's table of Commissioner-General figures; counts people classed Syrian, which includes Lebanese, Palestinians and Syrians proper.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 62

title: 2,920 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1900
why: Annual US arrivals classed Syrian, a count that includes Lebanese, Palestinians and Syrians proper.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: American Press prints 24 million pages in 1900
why: Of these 17,884,000 pages were Arabic Scriptures; the presses were idle two months for repairs and censors still cut Bible maps.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 694

title: Over a third of Mount Lebanon's people had emigrated since 1870
why: Jouplain estimates this and says some 12,000 emigrants a year sailed from Beirut, at least 400 at times on one ship.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 557

title: Syrian Protestant College enrols 512 students
why: Jessup notes steady growth year on year; the 1902 figure at Daniel Bliss's resignation was 626.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 694

title: Lebanon loses at least a quarter of its people to emigration
why: The Handbook calculates a fall of at least 100,000 in Lebanon's population between 1900 and 1914, mostly to the Americas and Egypt.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 186

title: 4,064 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1901
why: Arrivals rise by about 1,100 on 1900 in the US Commissioner-General's series.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: 4,982 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1902
why: Arrivals approach 5,000 for the first time in the series.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Syrian Protestant College had 626 students and 40 teachers at Bliss's resignation
why: Daniel Bliss led the college for 36 years, from sixteen students to five departments; instruction had switched from Arabic to English.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 216

title: Steam tramway carries Beirut's American community to Dog River
why: A special tram car took the party on Jessup's seventieth birthday picnic, showing the coast line was running by April 1902.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 709

title: Graduates give Daniel Bliss a gold medal on his resignation
why: Presented in the college Assembly Hall by students and resident graduates; graduates in Egypt and Sudan chose a marble statue instead.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 218

title: Howard Bliss lands in Beirut; father resigns college presidency to him
why: Daniel Bliss gave up the Syrian Protestant College presidency at the faculty meeting on the day his son arrived.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 216

title: 5,551 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1903
why: Highest annual count so far in the 1899-1919 series.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Syrian Protestant College enrolment reaches 629 in 1903
why: Enrolment table for the American College; it grew from 108 in 1880.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 201

title: Damascus cholera halts Beirut-Damascus railway traffic
why: Jessup says 1903 opened with cholera in Damascus and cordons stopped trains; an earlier 1890s cordon forced passengers into Beirut quarantine.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 719

title: Howard Bliss inauguration week; Daniel Bliss preaches his farewell sermon
why: The exercises ran Sunday 10 to Thursday 14 May 1903; the elder Bliss kept teaching Bible and ethics for four more years.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 216

title: Haiti bars entry of any person 'styled a Syrian'
why: The law excluded Syrians, including naturalised ones who left and returned; Haiti likened its case to US exclusion of Chinese.
cite: FRUS 1905, doc. 487, Haitian minister's note of 4 Sept 1905, p. 541

title: 3,653 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1904
why: Falls by almost 1,900 from 1903; counts cover everyone classed Syrian, not Lebanese alone.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Marble statue of Daniel Bliss unveiled at the college
why: Gift of graduates and former students in Egypt and the Sudan, carved in Italy from the living model; unveiled in spring 1904.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 220

title: Haiti promulgates its Syrian Exclusion Act
why: The Act of 1903 became law only on 8 June 1904; US minister later argued it could not apply to Syrians already trading.
cite: FRUS 1912, doc. 709, minister's despatch of 12 Feb 1912, p. 532

title: 4,822 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1905
why: Arrivals recover; a riot in the Manhattan Syrian quarter this year drew national press notice.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: American Press prints nearly 60 million pages, a Bible-printing record
why: Of these 47,275,000 pages were for the American Bible Society; 158,000 copies of Scripture issued, with demand from Egypt unprecedented.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 753

title: Emigration so large that farm labour runs short in Lebanon
why: Thirty years of emigration had by 1905 left too few hands for the corn, mulberry and vine; British Admiralty Handbook.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 186

title: Quarter of a million Syrians estimated to have emigrated since c.1875
why: About a quarter went to the US, 50,000 to South America, 25,000 to Central America, 10,000 to Australia, the rest to Africa and Asia.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 187

title: Riot in the Manhattan Syrian quarter runs for days
why: Hitti says it produced one murder and a few stabbings but national press notice; Hitti notes such outbreaks revive old feuds and sectarian divides.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 84

title: US rejects Haiti's reading that bars naturalised Syrian-origin Americans
why: Acting Secretary Loomis said the exclusion law was ambiguous on good-faith naturalised citizens; the case was Mansour Assaff's refused visa.

title: 5,824 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1906
why: Arrivals pass 5,800, a new high for the series.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: About 7,000 Syrian immigrants enter Argentina
why: Argentine official figure cited by the Admiralty Handbook; Syrian immigrants there took up peddling, then shops and farming.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 187

title: Aleppo-Rayak railway through the Bekaa opens to Aleppo
why: The Admiralty Handbook dates the opening of the railway to Rayak to 1906; its effect on Aleppo's imports shows from 1908.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 300

title: Only 58 Syrian college graduates live in the US, 87 in Egypt
why: Jessup's check of the 1906 catalogue found 145 of 1,387 graduates abroad; he argued English teaching was a minor cause of emigration.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 589

title: Syrian Protestant College enrolment reaches 769 in 1906
why: Graduates to 1906 total 300 in arts, 330 in medicine and 162 in pharmacy.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 201

title: Snow repeatedly blocks the Beirut-Damascus railway
why: Jessup says January 1906 brought storms, snow and sickness; the Damascus line was blocked several times.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 762

title: 5,880 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1907
why: Highest count so far; a 1907 Immigration Commission visit to Turkey recorded houses built with American money.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Beirut-Damascus road shows houses built with American money
why: A US Immigration Commission correspondent in 1907 said Syrians send more money home per head than any other nationality.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 54, quoting Immigration Commission vol. 12

title: Jessup says people were emigrating 'in thousands' from Ottoman misrule
why: He links the exodus to unpunished crime, secret police and censorship in the last year before the 1908 constitution.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 778

title: Corner-stones laid for an Orthodox bishop's college and the Wali's industrial schools
why: The Wali's schools opened, then closed after he was removed because they lacked endowment; the Greek college stalled for lack of funds.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 778

title: Imperial order gives Syrian Protestant College the immunities of other nations' schools
why: It covered the college and American schools across the empire; Jessup says the empire's censorship and spies remained.
cite: Jessup, Fifty-Three Years in Syria vol. II (1910), p. 778

title: Muzaffar Pasha dies; administrative council president takes charge
why: Jessup dates the death to 28 June, Jouplain to July; the Porte reused the 1892 interim formula until Yusuf Franko Pasha arrived in the autumn.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), p. 514 note 2; p. 507; Jessup vol. II (1910), p. 778
dup_of: Muzaffar Pasha dies; Yusuf Franko Pasha appointed mutasarrif

title: 5,520 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1908
why: Constitution year; the British Admiralty Handbook says the 1908 changes, including Christian conscription, raised emigration.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Beirut exports recorded at 919,200 pounds in 1908
why: Highest of the 1908-13 run in the consular series; the Handbook warns Beirut figures are understated.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 291, British consular returns (1913 footnote on p. 304)

title: Ottoman constitution raises emigration, partly to dodge conscription
why: The Handbook says confusion after 1908 and Christian and Jewish liability for military service pushed more people to leave.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 187

title: Ottoman import duty rises from 8% to 11%
why: The Handbook says imports paid 8% from 1862 to 1908 and 11% from 1908 to 1914, hitting Beirut's import-based trade.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 247

title: Paul Noujaim defends Paris law thesis 'La question du Liban'
why: Published as Jouplain, it is a full diplomatic history of the Mutasarrifate, still cited in 1919-20 French works.
cite: Jouplain (P. Noujaim), La question du Liban (Paris, 1908), title page; Samne, La Syrie (1920), p. 253 for the pseudonym

title: 95% of Syrian arrivals in 1908-09 join relatives or friends
why: Of 9,188 Syrians admitted in the two fiscal years, 8,725 said they were joining kin; chain migration drives the exodus.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 54, citing Reports of the Immigration Commission vol. 12, p. 59

title: 3,668 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1909
why: Sharp fall from 1908; Hitti notes 95% of 1908-09 arrivals joined relatives or friends.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Beirut exports recorded at 791,700 pounds in 1909
why: Falls from 1908 as silk and cereal exports weaken.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 291, British consular returns (1913 footnote on p. 304)

title: Beirut tramway requires conductors to speak French or English
why: The Electric Tramway Company of Beirut added the rule to the Arabic requirement, per the Admiralty Handbook.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 198

title: French lay mission opens a Beirut college to rival Saint Joseph
why: The Mission laique francaise opened it in 1909, as an explicitly secular French counterpart to the Jesuit university.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 200

title: Over 7,000 Syrian immigrants enter Argentina
why: Second peak year in the Argentine series; the Handbook adds that the 1908 constitution raised rather than cut emigration.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 187

title: Syrian Protestant College enrolment reaches 876 in 1909
why: The staff numbered 74 in 1908; three-quarters of students were Christian.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 201

title: Zahle's 'Brazil Street' named for emigrants' fortunes
why: In 1885 Zahle had one stone building, a church; by 1909 stone houses lined a street named for house-owners who made money in Brazil.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 178

title: 6,317 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1910
why: Highest count to date; the 1910 US census later counted only 46,727 people of Syrian and Arabic stock.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Beirut exports recorded at 822,500 pounds in 1910
why: Matches Baedeker's 1910 figure for Beirut exports.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 291, British consular returns (1913 footnote on p. 304)

title: Beirut port: 1,135 steamers of 1.7 million tons clear in 1910
why: Also 2,340 sailing vessels; exports were 822,500 pounds and, per Baedeker, imports 2,153,200 pounds, led by textiles and timber.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 282

title: Tripoli port: 661 steamers of 896,164 tons clear in 1910
why: Baedeker also lists 1,944 sailing ships of 41,444 tons; the 1909 imports were 300,000 pounds and exports 400,000 pounds.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 336

title: US census counts only 46,727 of Syrian and Arabic stock
why: Hitti calls this figure far too low; he estimates about 200,000 Syrians, foreign-born and born of Syrian parents, by 1919-20.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 62 and p. 65

title: 5,444 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1911
why: Annual arrivals stay above 5,000.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: About 20,000 emigrants leave Lebanon in 1911
why: Estimate in the British Admiralty Handbook; the rise from 1911 is blamed on new military service and the decline of silk.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 392

title: Beirut exports recorded at 550,500 pounds in 1911
why: Drop of a third on 1910; the Italian war and Balkan wars hurt Beirut most.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 291, British consular returns (1913 footnote on p. 304)

title: Concession to irrigate Kesrawan villages from the Nahr es-Salib
why: The Beirut Waterworks objected that it would lose water-power; the Porte ordered a commission to test the claim.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 410

title: Homs-Tripoli railway opens, giving Tripoli an inland rail link
why: The 64-mile French-built line ran Homs to Tripoli in four hours; the Admiralty Handbook says it gave Tripoli's trade 'a great impetus'.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 371; Admiralty Handbook (1920) p. 303

title: US minister reports Haiti prosecuting Syrian-origin retailers
why: Armed guards stood before stores, buyers were arrested and a Gonaives branch was closed, he wrote, in a campaign aimed only at Syrians.

title: 5,525 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1912
why: Arrivals level with 1911.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: 84,000 tons of Baghdad Railway rails move through Tripoli to Aleppo
why: Rails and 9,000 tons of coal went by the Homs line; Baghdad railway material shipped via Tripoli in 1913 was worth about 110,000 pounds.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 304

title: About 25,000 emigrants leave Lebanon in 1912
why: Estimate in the British Admiralty Handbook; the rise from 1911 is blamed on new military service and the decline of silk.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 392

title: Baedeker puts Beirut's population at 190,000
why: It counts 65,000 Moslems, 45,000 Orthodox, 40,000 Maronites and 3,500 Jews, plus 4,300 Europeans and a 2,000-strong garrison.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), pp. 281-282

title: Baedeker puts Tripoli's population at 30,000
why: The count is 24,000 Moslems, 4,500 Orthodox Greeks and 1,500 Maronites, in a liwa of the Beirut vilayet; El-Mina holds the port.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 336

title: Beirut exports recorded at 525,600 pounds in 1912
why: Lowest of the series; railways to Tripoli and Haifa cut Beirut's exports.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 291, British consular returns (1913 footnote on p. 304)

title: Beirut has 18 printing offices, 16 Arabic newspapers and 10 reviews
why: Baedeker calls the city the centre of the Oriental book trade in Syria, with the Jesuit and American presses the best.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 282

title: Beirut's electric trams run on four colour-coded lines
why: Red from Nahr Beirut to Khan Antun Bey, green to the Pine Wood, yellow to Furn esh-Shebak, blue to the Ras Beirut lighthouse.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 279

title: Beirut-Ma'amiltein light railway runs a train every three hours
why: The coast line ran from the harbour station past Nahr el-Kelb to Ma'amiltein, 12 miles in about 1 hr 15 min, Baedeker says.
cite: Baedeker, Palestine and Syria (1912 edition), p. 286

title: British consular report puts Mount Lebanon at 200,000 people
why: Other estimates in the Handbook run from 300,000 to 450,000; Cuinet's c.1900 total was 399,500, with 229,700 Maronites.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 392

title: By end-1912 most of Aleppo's imports pass through Tripoli
why: The Admiralty Handbook says the Homs-Tripoli line diverted a large share of Aleppo's trade from Alexandretta to Tripoli.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 303

title: Twenty-five Lebanese silk filatures closed down
why: Recorded in the British Admiralty Handbook's silk section; silk reeling was a mainstay of Mount Lebanon's economy.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 284

title: US tells Haiti to give Syrian firms time to liquidate
why: Haiti had refused to renew trader licences; it proposed six months and Washington judged that too short.

title: US declines British request to protest Haiti's Syrian trade ban
why: Washington said it saw no basis to dispute Haiti's right to exclude, and likened the law to US Chinese exclusion.

title: 9,210 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1913
why: Peak of the 1899-1919 series, the year before the war.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: About 30,000 emigrants leave Lebanon in 1913
why: Estimate in the British Admiralty Handbook; the rise from 1911 is blamed on new military service and the decline of silk.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 392

title: Beirut exports recorded at 630,800 pounds in 1913
why: Partial recovery; the Handbook says true exports were still above 800,000 pounds.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 291, British consular returns (1913 footnote on p. 304)

title: Estimate puts Beirut at 185,000 people, two-thirds Christian
why: The Handbook sets this against Cuinet's earlier estimate of 120,000, including 76,700 Christians.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 393

title: Tripoli's exports double in 1913 to about 800,000 pounds
why: Wool, hides, oranges, cocoons and olive oil exports more than doubled over 1912, per British consular figures; imports rose to about 1.25 million.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 304

title: Haiti's president claims expelled Syrians in Jamaica fund a revolution
why: The US minister doubted it; he noted Syrian-origin Americans were still being kept in business under an earlier licence arrangement.

title: Haiti says no Syrian-origin person may enter and stay
why: The president allowed naturalised US citizens of Syrian origin only brief business visits, certified by the State Department or legation.
cite: FRUS 1913, doc. 661, telegram of 25 July 1913

title: US consul in Kingston finds no Syrian plot against Haiti
why: He reported few Syrians in Jamaica held bank accounts and said most had lived there years, contradicting Haiti's claim.

title: Green dye test links Nahr es-Salib to the Jeita spring
why: The dye took six days to reach Jeita, under 10 miles away, and stayed visible for three days in the American College laboratory.
cite: Admiralty, Handbook of Syria (1920), p. 410

title: Haiti refuses further delay to Syrian-origin American trader Daniel John
why: He had been naturalised on 17 July 1906 and reached Haiti a week later; he got extensions to 30 November 1913.
cite: FRUS 1913, docs. 670 and 674

title: 1914 census of Mount Lebanon: 414,000 people, 233,000 of them Maronite
why: Components sum to 414,000, with 62,000 Greek Orthodox and 47,000 Druze; Adib Pasha thought the true total near 500,000.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), Annex I, from Adib Pasha
dup_of: 1913 census: Mount Lebanon 414,800 counted, 124,400 of them emigrants

title: 9,023 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1914
why: Second-highest count of the series, the year the Ottoman Empire entered the war.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Estimates of Syrian emigrants range from 570,000 to 1,000,000
why: The upper figure was thought to include children born abroad; no official totals existed, per the British Admiralty Handbook.
cite: Admiralty, A Handbook of Syria (including Palestine), 1920, p. 187

title: Ottomans abolish the Capitulations and tighten control of foreign schools
why: The sudden step ended foreigners' extra-territorial privileges; a new education law set strict supervision and stressed Turkish, per Bliss.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), pp. 225-226

title: Howard Bliss named US Deputy Marshal at the Beirut college
why: He and the faculty planned protection and defence of the campus, which he kept as an 'oasis of peace' through the war.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 226

title: Lebanese Committee in Paris 'implicitly dissolved'
why: Chekri Ganem later said it ended in December 1914 because of some members' stance; the Central Syrian Committee replaced it in June 1917.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 520, quoting Ganem's reply of 1918

title: US forms Palestine-Syrian Relief Committee for civilian famine
why: It raised funds through winter and spring 1915 and sent money to Palestine and Syria; later merged into the Armenian and Syrian relief body.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), p. 13

title: 1,767 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1915
why: Down from 9,023 in 1914 as the war and the Allied blockade of the coast take hold.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Howard Bliss wins terms for the college from Talaat and Enver
why: After the 1915 commencement he negotiated the foreign-schools law down to a workable adjustment; Djemal Pasha later showed goodwill.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 225

title: McMahon excludes districts west of Damascus, Homs, Hama, Aleppo from pledge
why: His letter to Sharif Hussein said those districts were not purely Arab.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 650

title: American Committee for Armenian and Syrian Relief formed
why: The Armenian Relief Committee absorbed the Persian and Palestine-Syrian committees; headquarters were at 70 Fifth Avenue, New York.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), p. 14
dup_of: US Syrian-Mount Lebanon Relief Committee formed (Najib Maalouf chair)

title: Sharif Hussein accepts exclusion of Mersin and Adana but claims Beirut
why: He kept the demand for the other territories, notably Beirut, in reply to McMahon's 24 October letter.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 650

title: 676 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1916
why: Lowest count so far; coincides with the famine in Mount Lebanon.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Batroun falls from 5,000 to 2,000 people by end of 1916
why: An eyewitness, Dr Joseph Ziade, said villages emptied; Marnema fell from 200 to 6 people, Abdelli from 2,000 to 150.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), pp. 439-440, quoting Ziade

title: Sharif Hussein defers his Lebanon claims until after the war
why: He wrote he would not press them during the war, to avoid disturbing the Franco-British alliance; McMahon acknowledged this on 30 January.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 650

title: US orders cruiser Des Moines to carry Red Cross party to Beirut
why: Lansing told the Piraeus-bound cruiser to take a Red Cross agent, seven Americans and hospital supplies to Beirut and seek Ottoman consent.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1212, telegram of 14 Jan 1916

title: Ottoman government refuses entry of ships to blockaded Beirut
why: Morgenthau cabled that with the Syrian coast blockaded by the Allied fleet the Porte would authorise no ships to enter Beirut.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1213, telegram of 17 Jan 1916

title: Ottomans specifically refuse the Des Moines a visit to Beirut
why: The Red Cross ship stayed at Alexandria; the Turkish Government had told the embassy the visit was not permitted.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1218, telegram of 13 Feb 1916

title: France refuses to ease Syrian coast blockade for a US relief ship
why: The French Minister of Marine told the US embassy a regularly declared blockade could not be modified to let the ship enter a blockaded port.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1223, telegram of 4 Apr 1916

title: Cairo press reports 150,000 dead of hunger in Lebanon by early May
why: The Journal du Caire, quoted by Samne, also said each person got 4 kg of barley and vetch flour per 26 days.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 437

title: France warns Washington of exactions and murders in Syria
why: A French note quoted by Lansing said reports described brutal treatment, exile and imprisonment and feared a methodical massacre as with the Armenians.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1113, pp. 850-851

title: Ottoman foreign minister says only families of executed men were deported
why: He told Philip that 20 Moslems and 2 Christians had been executed; the report adds French protege Emir Omar had reportedly been executed.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1116, telegram of 3 June 1916

title: US cable relays Cairo estimate of 80,000 starvation deaths in Lebanon
why: The State Department cable said a military cordon kept food out of Lebanon and that the distress was reportedly not wholly due to the war.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1232, telegram of 3 June 1916

title: US consul reports Lebanon deaths nearer 50,000; silk trade halted
why: Hollis in Beirut reduced the estimate; a private source told Philip silk, the main trade, had stopped for lack of men, money and transport.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1234, pp. 930-931

title: Lansing asks Turkey why it blocks Lebanon relief if none starve
why: He cabled Philip to ask what objections there were to sending relief to Syria and Lebanon if the Government was not trying to starve them.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1236, telegram of 24 June 1916

title: Ottoman foreign minister says no famine exists in Syria or Lebanon
why: He cited exceptionally good crops and said false reports came from people hoping to benefit from relief supplies, Philip reported.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1238, telegram of 6 July 1916

title: Washington warns that refusing Syrian relief could sour US opinion of Turkey
why: Acting Secretary Polk told the Ottoman government a refusal would not be understood and might affect American sentiment.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1237, telegram of 7 July 1916

title: Porte bars neutral relief; Djemal cites 3.5 million bushels sent
why: The foreign minister denied anyone had died of starvation and said Djemal asked for 10,000 pounds for the poor of Beirut and Lebanon.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1241, pp. 934-935

title: Daniel Bliss, founder of the Syrian Protestant College, dies in Beirut
why: He died at 11 a.m. on Thursday 27 July 1916; a service in the Mission Church followed the next day.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), pp. 254-255

title: Ottoman Bank delays emigrants' remittances, paying 80 piastres per pound
why: A reported rule: pay weekly instalments after a year in depreciated paper, against a market rate of 136; missionaries had carried the money.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), pp. 437-438, quoting wartime press

title: Porte rules out neutral relief committee; 20,000 pounds put at Djemal's disposal
why: Philip reported the cabinet decided this could not be permitted and said such relief was not essential; he asked for a Red Crescent plan.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1243, telegram of 12 Aug 1916 reporting an interview of 7 Aug

title: Porte accepts relief via Red Crescent and American Red Cross at Beirut
why: The Sublime Porte told Philip it had no objection to distribution to the poor of Syria through those two bodies.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1248, telegram of 9 Sept 1916

title: Beirut Red Cross chapter offers 25 men and 15 women
why: Consul-General Hollis said they wanted a controlling voice and that Syrians need wheat, not flour, plus sugar, rice, coffee and oil.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1249, telegram of 16 Sept 1916

title: Relief ship Caesar chartered; Djemal Pasha demands it land at Jaffa
why: He wanted the food consigned to him; the cargo was diverted to Alexandria and sold, the proceeds sent to Beirut for relief.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), p. 74
dup_of: US collier Caesar leaves with $250,000 relief for Mount Lebanon

title: Navy plans collier to carry Syrian relief food
why: Lansing demanded assurances that the Red Cross would have controlling management of distribution before the ship sailed.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1250, telegram of 14 Oct 1916

title: Ottomans agree to duty-free relief food for Beirut
why: After prolonged negotiation Ambassador Elkus obtained consent to supplies consigned to the Beirut consul general and shared out with Red Crescent.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1253, telegram of 23 Nov 1916

title: France grants free passage through the blockade to the collier Caesar
why: The French ambassador said Paris warned it could not repeat such exceptions and asked for the cargo and landing port to be notified.
cite: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 1252, note of 25 Nov 1916

title: Death rate in Syria jumps when the Caesar relief ship fails
why: Dr Graham of the Beirut medical school said hopes of American food had buoyed people for months; thousands gave up on the news.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), p. 74

title: 976 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1917
why: Arrivals stay below 1,000 while Ottoman rule and the blockade continue.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: College suspended for two weeks after US-Turkey diplomatic break
why: Teaching stopped 22 April to 7 May 1917 except the nurses' school; the college then reopened and never closed again.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 226

title: State Department lists Caesar relief cargo: 825,000 lb wheat, 980,000 lb flour
why: Hoffman Philip reported minor cargo damage on the voyage to Alexandria; some sugar was sold and much purchased relief food stayed in New York.
cite: FRUS 1918 Supplement 2, doc. 668, letter of 4 May 1917, pp. 545-546
dup_of: US collier Caesar leaves with $250,000 relief for Mount Lebanon

title: US consul Chesborough leaves Beirut, reporting starvation and typhus
why: His account: starvation across Syria; a municipal doctor counted 7,000+ typhus cases in Beirut, 40 deaths daily; Samne cites 600,000 dead overall.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 439

title: French naval officer's letter: 40-50 starvation victims collected daily in Beirut
why: He also reported weekly Beirut-Damascus trains and fruit trees cut for locomotive fuel; a private wartime letter quoted in 1920.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 438, letter of 1 July 1917

title: 210 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1918
why: Lowest count of the series, in the last year of the war and the famine.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Antoura orphanage holds 650 of 2,000 children the Turks tried to Turkify
why: Near East Relief planned further orphanages at Sidon, Beirut, Brummana and Tripoli in the winter of 1918.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), p. 75

title: Beirut civil governor Azmi Bey, hostile to the college, resigns
why: Bliss says Azmi Bey relaxed his hostility before resigning in summer 1918; the college got wheat at army rates from the Government.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 226

title: Mothers made to choose which children live in Lebanese villages
why: James Nicol reported villages applied 'survival of the fittest' in relief; Sidon district alone held about 5,000 destitute children.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), p. 75

title: First French administrators reach Beirut
why: Samne says Commandant Doizelet became military governor on 20 October and began food provisioning on 22 October.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 480

title: French food administration opens in Beirut with 126 staff
why: Samne says it began 22 October 1918 with 126 employees and about 100 handlers to feed the starved population.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 480

title: 231 Syrian immigrants enter the United States in 1919
why: First postwar year; arrivals are still near the war-time low.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), pp. 62-65, table from Commissioner-General of Immigration, annual report 1919, p. 168

title: Mount Lebanon Relief Committee has raised $165,815.58 in America
why: Raised in two and a half years from about 15,000 Syrian subscribers; Hitti says more went through the papal legation and Spanish embassy.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 87

title: Howard Bliss goes to Paris to press Syrian self-determination
why: He stayed several weeks and addressed the Council of Ten at the Peace Conference, then sailed for the US ill in March.
cite: Bliss, The Reminiscences of Daniel Bliss (1920), p. 227

title: Daoud Ammoun asks Paris for a Lebanon within natural frontiers
why: Le Temps published his statement: a Lebanon free of constraint, restored to its natural frontiers, with France's help.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 231, citing Le Temps of 29 Jan 1919

title: Red Cross hands Syria and Palestine relief to Near East Relief
why: The agreement signed at Konia took effect 1 April 1919 and added Palestine to the area administered by Near East Relief.
cite: Barton, Story of Near East Relief (1930), pp. 77-78

title: Lebanon's Official Journal publishes council's claim to detached territories
why: The Administrative Council resolved that parts taken from Mount Lebanon should return, citing historic limits and Entente promises.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 560
dup_of: Administrative Council declares Lebanon's independence within its borders

title: British military police arrest Emir Said in Beirut, ship him to Egypt
why: A French account says it happened with no French authority present, on Allenby's order; Said was a grandson of Abd el-Kader.
cite: Samne, La Syrie (Paris, 1920), p. 565

title: Commission credits American-earned money for Lebanon's roads and stone houses
why: The report links Lebanon's relative prosperity to emigrant remittances, and to freedom from conscription and light taxes.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), p. 776

title: Commission finds Druzes want to stay out of a French-ruled Lebanon
why: It also reported that most Sunni and Shia and many Orthodox in Tyre, Sidon, the Bekaa and Tripoli opposed French rule.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), p. 775

title: Commission says Maronite official line opposes becoming part of France
why: Even many pro-French Lebanese rejected annexation to France, the report said; it urged local autonomy within a united Syria.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), pp. 776-777

title: In the French-run western zone, 196 of 446 petitions seek Greater Lebanon
why: That is 43.9%; 108 (24.2%) opposed it, 33 wanted an autonomous Lebanon in Syria and 187 (41.9%) wanted a united Syria.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), p. 759

title: King-Crane recommend Syrian unity; a French mandate over Lebanon 'possible'
why: The report urged local autonomy for Lebanon within Syria, and said if France pressed, a mandate over an unenlarged Lebanon was an arrangement, not recommended.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), p. 799

title: King-Crane tally: 203 of 1,863 Syrian petitions back independent Greater Lebanon
why: The commission counted 1,062 petitions (57.0%) against it and 33 for an autonomous Lebanon inside a Syrian state.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), p. 761

title: King-Crane: French mandate first choice for 274 petitions, 215 from Lebanon
why: The commission recorded 14.68% choosing France, all but 59 from the Lebanon district, against 1,129 (60.5%) for America.
cite: FRUS 1919 Paris Peace Conference vol. XII, doc. 380 (King-Crane report), p. 769

title: Presbyterian Board has sent $2.25 million from Syrians in America
why: The Board transmitted $2,250,362.07 to relatives in Syria by 1 Dec 1919; a major channel of wartime and famine remittance.
cite: Hitti, The Syrians in America (1924), p. 87
